column1: # Whizbang performance baseline. One measure per line, tab separated:
#   name<TAB>value<TAB>unit<TAB>ceiling<TAB>note
# The value is what the measure read when the line was last written, and is reported as drift on
# every run. The CEILING is the gate, and is deliberately optional: a measure with no ceiling is
# recorded and never fails a run. Declare one only where the number is a property of the design
# rather than of the machine, and say why in the note -- a ceiling that encodes a machine's speed
# will either flap or hide a real regression, which is the failure mode this file exists to avoid.
# Values are WORK DONE (tuples, scans, blocks, rows), never wall clock. Time moves with the runner,
# its neighbors and its cache; a plan's page and tuple counts do not.
# Eight streams carrying 2,500 settled rows each in all three queue tables, none of them in the
# stream ledger, so every ring takes the deterministic-target branch. A ring names streams and must
# cost what it names, never what those streams have accumulated.
# Before the deterministic branch stopped recovering a stream's partition number by reading the
# queue table, the same scenario read 20,000 tuples and took one sequential scan PER RING on each
# of the three branches. That is the measurement this suite exists to have caught.
# The ceiling is on tuples read, and it is a property of the design: the partition number is a
# total function of the stream id, so a ring has no reason to read a queue row at all. A hundred
# leaves room for a planner that reads a page to answer something else while still being two orders
# of magnitude below a scan of a 20,000-row table. Scan counts are recorded without a ceiling,
# because they are the same finding counted a second way and one gate per family is enough.
doorbell.inbox.wh_inbox.seq_scans_per_ring
column5: was 1 per ring before the fix

column5: was 20000 per ring; a ring must not read a queue row

column1: # --- Store emptiness probe against a pending backlog -----------------------------------------
# 200 streams carrying 100 pending unpublished outbox rows each, then a producer storing four
# messages per call on streams the outbox has never held. Before its first insert for a stream the
# store asks whether that stream has a pending row, so it knows whether to ring a doorbell.
# The ceiling is on tuples read per ROW WRITTEN, which is the ratio a deployed fleet reported at
# 4,550 and the one that makes a scan obvious whatever the absolute size of the table: a store
# should read about what it writes. Fifty leaves room for the small bookkeeping tables the store
# legitimately reads while being two orders of magnitude below a scan.
# The absolute per-call tuple count carries a ceiling too, because the ratio alone can be satisfied
# by a call that writes more rather than by one that reads less.
# Measured before the fix: 80,078 tuples and 4 sequential scans per call, 20,019.5 tuples per row
# written. Every stream_id index on wh_outbox is partial on a condition this predicate cannot
# satisfy, so nothing served it and it scanned every unpublished row to prove a fresh stream empty.
# The perspective measures below were noise until wh_perspective_events was seeded. The same loop
# probes that table, and the fixture left it EMPTY, so the measure read four sequential scans of
# nothing and zero tuples. A scan of an empty table is what the planner picks for an empty table,
# and it is indistinguishable in these counters from a probe answered by an index. A measure taken
# against a table the fixture never fills reads as clean whether the defect is there or not, and a
# gate that cannot fail is worse than no gate because it is counted as coverage. Seeded, the same
# measure prices a real probe and the four scans become none.
# Being exact about what this gate does and does not cover: it stores to FRESH streams only, so it
# exercises one of the probe's three stream states. It would NOT have caught the drained-stream
# defect, which is why that lives in its own scenario below with all three states measured
# separately. Seeding this one makes its number mean something; it does not make it sufficient.
store.rows_written_per_call
store.wh_outbox.seq_scans_per_call
column5: was 4 per call before the fix, one per fresh stream

column5: was 80078; a probe by stream id must not read the table

# The gate is the MULTIPLE, because it is the only measure that separates a poll that is expensive
# because it was asked for a lot from a poll that is expensive because of what it happened to find.
# A poll bounded by the batch it was asked for holds this near one. Two leaves room for the larger
# table's own index depth while still failing a poll whose cost tracks its consumer's data shape.

# --- Store perspective emptiness probe, by stream state ---------------------------------------
# 200 streams holding 100 pending perspective events each, plus one stream carrying 400 PROCESSED
# events and nothing pending, plus store calls on stream ids the table has never held. One message
# per call, so exactly one stream is probed per call, and one stream state per measured window.
# The three states exist as separate measures because averaging them is how this defect stayed
# hidden. Migration 160 recorded this probe as costing three buffers, which was true of a stream the
# table had never held and false of a stream whose work was all done. A drained stream is what every
# long-lived stream becomes and what it stays between bursts, so it is the common state rather than
# an edge, and it was the one that read the whole table.
# Measured before the fix, on the drained stream: 337.8 blocks and 20,400 tuples for ONE probe, from a
# sequential scan the planner chose because processed_at IS NULL is true of nearly every row, so it
# expected to stop at the first one. There is no match on a drained stream, so it read all of them.
# The ceiling is declared ONCE and applies to all three states, which is the property worth gating:
# what the probe costs follows the question asked, not the history the stream happens to carry. A
# ceiling that held only for a fresh stream is the measurement that missed this the first time.
# Sequential scans carry the tightest gate because the defect is binary -- an index answers it or a
# scan does -- and half a scan per call is not a thing that can happen.
probe.wh_perspective_events.blocks_per_call.drained
column5: was 337.8; a drained stream read the whole table

column1: # --- Claim write cost, narrow state row versus the wide row it replaced ------------------------
# 20,000 rows each side, 500 stamped per measured batch. The BEFORE side is reconstructed -- a row
# of the same width carrying the same moved columns and the indexes the cutover removed -- because
# after the cutover the comparison no longer exists: the message row has no mutable columns left to
# stamp. Synthetic on identity, faithful on the two dimensions that drive the cost.
# An update can only take PostgreSQL cheap in-place path when it touches NO indexed column and the
# page has room. Claiming writes indexed columns by definition, so that path is unreachable and the
# index count IS the cost. Blocks per row stamped, never wall clock.
# The gate is the state row INDEX COUNT, because that is the thing a future change trades away
# without noticing: the plan carried 69 percent off every write, measured when the state table held
# six indexes, and restoring the five priority lanes took it to eleven and the reduction to 51.
# Twelve leaves room for one more lane while failing a drift back toward the seventeen the wide row
# carried. The reduction percent is recorded and NOT gated, because a ceiling is an upper bound and
# this number wants a floor; the ratio is asserted in the test instead, at 1.5x.
claim_write.wide_row.blocks_per_row
column5: recorded, not gated: the shape the split replaced, kept so the pair reads as a before and after

column1: claim_write.wide_row.indexes
column5: recorded: the index set the cutover removed

column1: claim_write.state_row.blocks_per_row
column5: recorded, not gated: follows the index count below, which is the gate

column1: claim_write.state_row.indexes
column5: GATED: a design property. The write win IS the index count on the hot table; 6 indexes gave 69 percent off, 11 gives 51, and a return toward 17 gives back the whole reason the split exists

column1: claim_write.reduction_percent
column5: recorded, not gated: a ceiling cannot express a floor. The test asserts the wide/narrow ratio exceeds 1.5x; measured 2.03x

column1: # --- Maintenance row-expiry reap, nothing expired ---------------------------------------------
# 24 perspective tables holding 500 unexpired rows each, of which 2 declare a row lifetime in the
# registry. Both discovery shapes run against the same fixture so the pair reads as a before and
# after, the way the ephemeral reap scenario drops and recreates its index. Only wh_per_* tables are
# measured, so the cycle's other twelve tasks stay out of the number.
# expires_at comes from the shared perspective table template, so EVERY perspective table has the
# column whether or not its perspective declares a lifetime. Finding tables by asking the catalog for
# that column therefore selected all of them and issued an unindexed DELETE against each. The
# predicate matched nothing -- a perspective that declares no lifetime never stamps the column -- but
# not matching still read every row of every table.
# Measured on a deployed service before the change: 120 tables scanned for the 3 that declare a
# lifetime, 14,758 ms to delete zero rows, against 377 ms for the other twelve maintenance tasks
# combined. perform_maintenance was the heaviest statement on that database by total time, averaging
# 19.2 s and 615k buffers a call, and 98 percent of it was this one task. Two other services scanned
# 81 tables for one declaring perspective and 32 for nine.
# The gate is TABLES SCANNED, because that is a property of the design rather than of the machine:
# the reap has no reason to read a table whose perspective never declared a lifetime, whatever the
# planner or the hardware does. Four leaves room for another declaring perspective in the fixture
# while failing any drift back toward sweeping all 24. Tuples read is the same finding counted a
# second way, gated loosely so it cannot be satisfied by reading fewer rows from more tables.
# Residual, recorded here rather than hidden: the DELETE against a DECLARING table is still
# unindexed, because expires_at carries no index. That is proportionate now -- three tables on the
# service above rather than a hundred and twenty -- but a service with many declaring perspectives
# holding large tables would want an index on the column, and this is the measure that would show it.
maintenance.ttl_reap.catalog_sweep.tables_scanned_per_cycle
column5: recorded, not gated: the shape the registry replaces, kept so the pair reads as a before and after

column1: maintenance.ttl_reap.catalog_sweep.tuples_read_per_cycle
column5: recorded, not gated: every row of every table, to prove nothing was expired

column1: maintenance.ttl_reap.registry.tables_scanned_per_cycle
column5: GATED: a design property. The reap reads the registry, so it touches only the perspectives that declare a row lifetime; a return toward 24 is the catalog sweep coming back

column1: maintenance.ttl_reap.registry.tuples_read_per_cycle
column5: GATED: the declaring tables are still read in full, since expires_at is unindexed. The ceiling fails a sweep of the non-declaring ones without pretending the residual scan is free

column1: # --- Outbox claim, an urgent row behind a bulk backlog -----------------------------------------
# 5,000 bulk rows across 500 streams, all leased by the instance and queued an hour earlier, then
# one interactive row queued last. Arrival order alone would return the urgent row 5,001st, so it
# would never be claimed while the backlog lasted -- which is the symptom this fix exists for: a
# reply someone is waiting for published behind whatever bulk work was queued before it.
# The corpus rule asserts the ORDER BY exists, which is a property of the text. This measures the
# OUTCOME, because an ORDER BY can be present and still not be honoured if a plan or an index
# changes underneath it.
# The gate is POSITION, and it is a design property: an interactive row is the most urgent thing the
# instance holds, so it comes first. There is no tolerance to give -- second place means the
# ordering is in the text and not in the plan.
# Blocks and scans are RECORDED and NOT gated, deliberately. The cost property -- that a poll is
# priced by the batch rather than by what the instance holds -- belongs to
# ClaimWorkPlanShapeTests, which fixes row width and holdings for that purpose and which caught
# this very change regressing to 1,272 blocks against its 1,200 ceiling on the first attempt. Two
# ceilings on one property would drift apart, and a ceiling here would be measured against a
# fixture chosen to demonstrate ordering rather than cost.
outbox_priority.urgent_row_position
column5: GATED: a design property. An interactive row is the most urgent thing the instance holds; arrival order alone would place it 5001st

column1: outbox_priority.claim.blocks_per_call
column5: recorded, not gated: the cost gate is ClaimWorkPlanShapeTests, which fixes width and holdings for it

column1: outbox_priority.claim.seq_scans_per_call
column5: recorded, not gated: same reason

column1: # --- Idle band, busy poll behind a withheld backlog -----------------------------------------
# 20,000 fresh idle-band rows behind 500 ordinary pending rows, polled as a BUSY service, so not
# one idle row may be taken. The band adds a fourth bucket and an admission probe to a function
# every instance calls several times a second; if either reads the band, the feature charges the
# whole fleet for the size of the backlog it is withholding, and does so more the better it works.
# The absolute block counts are recorded without a ceiling: they move with page fill and with what
# the fixture left behind, which is exactly the kind of number this file says not to gate on. The
# DIFFERENCE between the two polls is a property of the design, and carries the ceiling.
# Measured: 2 sequential tuples, not 20,000 -- the probe is answered by walking an index to the
# first qualifying entry. The withheld band cost 125 blocks, against the ~3,700 a poll costs
# anyway.
idle_band.busy_poll.blocks_per_call
column5: absolute cost moves with the machine; the delta below is the gate
